CALIFORNIA HOMEOWNER BILL OF RIGHTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — INFORMATIONAL ONLY
This information sheet describes, in general terms, borrower-protection provisions of California's Homeowner Bill of Rights that constrain how a mortgage servicer may pursue foreclosure of certain residential loans, codified principally at California Civil Code §§ 2923.5, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.11, 2924.12, 2924.15, and 2924.18. It concerns a loan secured by the real property commonly known as 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, on which Pat Morgan is identified as borrower and Example Mortgage Lending, Inc. as beneficiary (lender); the loan is currently serviced by Example Loan Servicing, Inc., loan number 0012345678. This sheet summarizes, at a general level: the pre-foreclosure borrower-contact requirement that must be satisfied before a notice of default may be recorded; the prohibition on recording a notice of default or notice of sale, or conducting a trustee's sale, while a complete first-lien loan-modification application is pending (sometimes called "dual tracking"); the requirement that a servicer establish a single point of contact once a borrower requests a foreclosure prevention alternative; the statutory scope limits and small-servicer exemption that determine which loans and which servicers these provisions reach; and the statutory remedies available for a material violation. It is a companion to — and does not duplicate or replace — an information sheet describing California's general nonjudicial foreclosure process under Civil Code § 2924 et seq. (the notice of default's statutory content, the waiting period before a notice of sale, the right of reinstatement, and the antideficiency rule); the protections summarized in this sheet operate as additional requirements layered on top of, not in substitution for, that general process. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself contact any borrower, evaluate or approve any loan modification or other foreclosure prevention alternative, establish or designate any single point of contact, record or rescind any notice, or determine whether any mortgage servicer's actual conduct toward this or any other loan has complied — or failed to comply — with any statute described here.

STATUTORY SCOPE — OWNER-OCCUPIED LOANS SECURED BY A FIRST LIEN
The Homeowner Bill of Rights provisions summarized in this sheet do not apply to every residential mortgage loan. California Civil Code § 2924.15(a) provides: "Unless otherwise provided, paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) of Section 2924 and Sections 2923.5, 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, and 2924.18 shall apply only to a first lien mortgage or deed of trust that is secured by owner-occupied residential real property containing no more than four dwelling units." "Owner-occupied" carries a defined meaning for this purpose: Section 2924.15(b) provides that "[f]or purposes of this section, 'owner-occupied' means that the property is the principal residence of the borrower and is security for a loan made for personal, family, or household purposes." As applied to the loan secured by 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, whether that property is the principal residence of Pat Morgan and whether the loan identified as 0012345678 is a first-lien loan made for personal, family, or household purposes determines whether the pre-foreclosure contact, dual-tracking, single-point-of-contact, and related requirements described in this sheet apply to that loan at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Unless otherwise provided, paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) of Section 2924 and Sections 2923.5, 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, and 2924.18 shall apply only to a first lien mortgage or deed of trust that is secured by owner-occupied residential real property containing no more than four dwelling units."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2924.15(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 2924.15(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2924.15.&lawCode=CIV)
  "For purposes of this section, “owner-occupied” means that the property is the principal residence of the borrower and is security for a loan made for personal, family, or household purposes."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2924.15(b) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 2924.15(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2924.15.&lawCode=CIV)
  Known gap: This is California statutory law, used as real evidence of that state's Homeowner Bill of Rights scope limits — not a determination of which state's law governs any specific loan, nor a determination that the property and loan identified on this sheet in fact meet the owner-occupied, first-lien, four-or-fewer-unit definition this section requires. Both quoted passages are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 2924.15, subdivisions (a) and (b) — they are quoted together, rather than as independent sources, because subdivision (b) directly defines a term used in subdivision (a).

PRE-FORECLOSURE BORROWER CONTACT REQUIRED BEFORE A NOTICE OF DEFAULT
Before a notice of default may be recorded against a covered loan such as the one secured by 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, California Civil Code § 2923.5(a)(1) requires that a mortgage servicer first make contact, or satisfy a due-diligence standard for attempting contact, with the borrower. As enacted, subdivision (a)(1)(A) requires "[e]ither 30 days after initial contact is made as required by paragraph (2) or 30 days after satisfying the due diligence requirements as described in subdivision (e)" before a notice of default pursuant to Section 2924 may be recorded. The required contact itself is described in subdivision (a)(2)(A): "A mortgage servicer shall contact the borrower in person or by telephone in order to assess the borrower's financial situation and explore options for the borrower to avoid foreclosure." During that contact, the mortgage servicer must advise the borrower of the right to request a follow-up meeting (to be scheduled within 14 days) and must provide the toll-free HUD housing-counseling referral number. A recorded notice of default must include a declaration that the mortgage servicer has contacted the borrower, tried with due diligence to do so, or that no contact was required. Whether Example Loan Servicing, Inc. has made or attempted the contact this section describes with respect to Pat Morgan concerning the loan secured by 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 is not addressed by this sheet.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2923.5(a)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 2923.5(a)(1)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2923.5.&lawCode=CIV)
  "A mortgage servicer shall contact the borrower in person or by telephone in order to assess the borrower’s financial situation and explore options for the borrower to avoid foreclosure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2923.5(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 2923.5(a)(2)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2923.5.&lawCode=CIV)

Both quoted passages are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 2923.5, subdivisions (a)(1)(A) and (a)(2)(A) — they are quoted together, rather than as independent sources, because they describe the timing rule and the substantive contact requirement it is measured from within one integrated provision. This section applies only to the class of loans described in Civil Code § 2924.15 (see the scope clause of this sheet) and only to entities described in subdivision (b) of Civil Code § 2924.18 (see the scope/exemption clause of this sheet); it does not apply universally to every residential mortgage servicer or loan.

PROHIBITION ON PURSUING FORECLOSURE WHILE A COMPLETE LOAN MODIFICATION APPLICATION IS PENDING ("DUAL TRACKING")
Two separate, independently numbered Civil Code sections restrict a mortgage servicer from pursuing foreclosure of a covered loan while a complete first-lien loan-modification application submitted by the borrower is pending — a practice sometimes referred to as "dual tracking." Civil Code § 2923.6(c) provides: "If a borrower submits a complete application for a first lien loan modification offered by, or through, the borrower's mortgage servicer at least five business days before a scheduled foreclosure sale, a mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall not record a notice of default or notice of sale, or conduct a trustee's sale, while the complete first lien loan modification application is pending." A separately numbered section, Civil Code § 2924.18(a)(1), independently imposes an overlapping prohibition: "If a borrower submits a complete application for a first lien loan modification offered by, or through, the borrower's mortgage servicer at least five business days before a scheduled foreclosure sale, a mortgage servicer, trustee, mortgagee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall not record a notice of default, notice of sale, or conduct a trustee's sale while the complete first lien loan modification application is pending, and until the borrower has been provided with a written determination by the mortgage servicer regarding that borrower's eligibility for the requested loan modification." Section 2923.6 also sets out a longer sequence of follow-on protections not quoted here — including a borrower's right to appeal a denial and specific content requirements for a denial notice — that apply only where Section 2923.6 itself applies (see the scope/exemption clause of this sheet); Section 2924.18(a)'s dual-tracking prohibition applies more broadly and is not subject to that same carve-out.

The two quoted passages are drawn from two separate, independently numbered Civil Code sections — § 2923.6(c) and § 2924.18(a)(1) — and are genuinely independent of each other, not subdivisions of a single section; they are quoted together because they impose substantially overlapping dual-tracking prohibitions that apply to a different scope of servicers (see the small-servicer exemption clause of this sheet, under which § 2923.6(c)-(h) does not apply to small servicers described in § 2924.18(b), while § 2924.18(a) itself is not subject to that same carve-out). Both sections apply only to the class of loans described in Civil Code § 2924.15 (see the scope clause of this sheet).

SINGLE POINT OF CONTACT ONCE A FORECLOSURE PREVENTION ALTERNATIVE IS REQUESTED
California Civil Code § 2923.7(a) requires: "When a borrower requests a foreclosure prevention alternative, the mortgage servicer shall promptly establish a single point of contact and provide to the borrower one or more direct means of communication with the single point of contact." The single point of contact is a defined role with specific statutory duties, not merely a named individual: it must, among other things, communicate the application process and deadlines, coordinate receipt of application documents, stay informed of the current status of the borrower's foreclosure prevention alternative, ensure the borrower is considered for all alternatives the servicer offers, and — as Section 2923.7(b)(5) specifically provides — have "access to individuals with the ability and authority to stop foreclosure proceedings when necessary." The single point of contact must remain assigned to the borrower's account until the servicer determines that all loss mitigation options have been exhausted or the account becomes current, and the servicer must ensure the single point of contact refers the borrower to a supervisor on request, if the single point of contact has one. Whether Example Loan Servicing, Inc. has established a single point of contact for Pat Morgan in connection with the loan secured by 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 is not addressed by this sheet.

Both quoted passages are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 2923.7, subdivisions (a) and (b)(5) — they are quoted together, rather than as independent sources, because subdivision (b) defines the duties of the single point of contact that subdivision (a) requires the servicer to establish. This section applies only to the class of loans described in Civil Code § 2924.15 and does not apply to certain small servicers (see the scope/exemption clause of this sheet).

SMALL-SERVICER EXEMPTION FROM CERTAIN HOMEOWNER BILL OF RIGHTS PROVISIONS
Not every mortgage servicer is subject to every Homeowner Bill of Rights provision described in this sheet. Civil Code § 2924.18(b) defines two categories of smaller-volume servicers to which certain sections apply on different terms. The first category, under paragraph (1), is: "A depository institution chartered under state or federal law, a person licensed pursuant to Division 9 (commencing with Section 22000) or Division 20 (commencing with Section 50000) of the Financial Code, or a person licensed pursuant to Part 1 (commencing with Section 10000) of Division 4 of the Business and Professions Code, that, during its immediately preceding annual reporting period, as established with its primary regulator, foreclosed on 175 or fewer residential real properties, containing no more than four dwelling units, that are located in California." The second category, under paragraph (2), is: "A person or entity that services seven or fewer loans encumbering residential real property located in California in a calendar year." A separately numbered section, Civil Code § 2923.6(i), then carves entities meeting that definition out of the dual-tracking and appeal provisions described elsewhere in this sheet: "Subdivisions (c) to (h), inclusive, shall not apply to entities described in subdivision (b) of Section 2924.18." California Civil Code § 2924.18(c) further provides that if a small servicer within the meaning of paragraph (1) later exceeds the 175-foreclosure threshold, it must notify its primary regulator and any delinquent borrower of the date — the first day of the sixth month after the close of the relevant reporting period — on which it becomes subject to Sections 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, and 2924.12. Whether Example Loan Servicing, Inc. falls within either category described in Section 2924.18(b), and therefore whether the dual-tracking, single-point-of-contact, and related provisions described in this sheet reach the servicing of the loan secured by 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, is not addressed by this sheet.

The three quoted passages are drawn from two separate, independently numbered Civil Code sections — § 2924.18(b) (its two paragraphs, (1) and (2), quoted separately but not independent of each other since both are subdivisions of the same statutory sentence) and § 2923.6(i), which is independent of § 2924.18(b) — they are quoted together because § 2924.18(b) supplies the definition that § 2923.6(i) applies. This exemption, by its own terms, reaches only the specific sections it lists (§§ 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, and 2924.12) — it does not, on this sheet's reading of the statutory text, exempt a small servicer from the pre-foreclosure contact requirement of § 2923.5 or from § 2924.18's own dual-tracking prohibition, both of which are discussed in separate clauses of this sheet.

STATUTORY REMEDIES FOR A MATERIAL VIOLATION
California Civil Code § 2924.12 creates a private right of action for a material violation of certain Homeowner Bill of Rights provisions, and the remedy available differs depending on whether a trustee's sale has already occurred. Before a sale, Section 2924.12(a)(1) provides: "If a trustee's deed upon sale has not been recorded, a borrower may bring an action for injunctive relief to enjoin a material violation of Section 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, or 2924.17." Any such injunction remains in place until the violation is corrected and remedied. After a trustee's deed upon sale has been recorded, Section 2924.12(b) instead provides a damages remedy: "a mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall be liable to a borrower for actual economic damages pursuant to Section 3281, resulting from a material violation of Section 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, or 2924.17 by that mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent where the violation was not corrected and remedied prior to the recordation of the trustee's deed upon sale. If the court finds that the material violation was intentional or reckless, or resulted from willful misconduct by a mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent, the court may award the borrower the greater of treble actual damages or statutory damages of fifty thousand dollars ($50,000)." A prevailing borrower may also recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs, and a violation of the listed sections by certain state-licensed persons is separately deemed a violation of that person's licensing law.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2924.12(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 2924.12(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2924.12.&lawCode=CIV)

Both quoted passages are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 2924.12, subdivisions (a)(1) and (b) — they are quoted together, rather than as independent sources, because they describe the pre-sale and post-sale phases of a single remedy scheme. As this sheet reads the statutory text, Section 2924.12's private right of action is expressly limited to material violations of the sections it lists by number — §§ 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, and 2924.17 — which does not, on its face, include a violation of the pre-foreclosure contact requirement of § 2923.5 or of § 2924.18's own dual-tracking prohibition; this sheet does not resolve what remedy, if any, exists for a violation of those two sections specifically, and that question is not addressed further here. Civil Code § 2924.12(i) further provides that this remedy section does not apply to entities described in subdivision (b) of Section 2924.18 (see the small-servicer exemption clause of this sheet), and Section 2924.12(e) provides that no violation affects the validity of a sale to a bona fide purchaser for value without notice.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT — INFORMATIONAL SHEET ONLY
I have reviewed this information sheet describing borrower-protection provisions of California's Homeowner Bill of Rights applicable to certain residential mortgage loans, including the loan secured by 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 and serviced by Example Loan Servicing, Inc. I understand that this document is informational only: it does not itself contact any borrower, evaluate or approve any loan modification or other foreclosure prevention alternative, establish or designate any single point of contact, record or rescind any notice, initiate, halt, or affect any specific foreclosure, or determine whether Example Loan Servicing, Inc.'s actual conduct toward this or any other loan has complied with the statutory requirements it describes. I further understand that this sheet is a companion to — not a substitute for — an information sheet describing California's general nonjudicial foreclosure process, and that whether the loan identified as 0012345678 meets the owner-occupied, first-lien scope requirement described in this sheet, and whether Example Loan Servicing, Inc. meets any small-servicer exemption described in this sheet, are not addressed or determined by this document.

expectedJSON.body: Two separate, independently numbered Civil Code sections restrict a mortgage servicer from pursuing foreclosure of a covered loan while a complete first-lien loan-modification application submitted by the borrower is pending — a practice sometimes referred to as "dual tracking." Civil Code § 2923.6(c) provides: "If a borrower submits a complete application for a first lien loan modification offered by, or through, the borrower's mortgage servicer at least five business days before a scheduled foreclosure sale, a mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall not record a notice of default or notice of sale, or conduct a trustee's sale, while the complete first lien loan modification application is pending." A separately numbered section, Civil Code § 2924.18(a)(1), independently imposes an overlapping prohibition: "If a borrower submits a complete application for a first lien loan modification offered by, or through, the borrower's mortgage servicer at least five business days before a scheduled foreclosure sale, a mortgage servicer, trustee, mortgagee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall not record a notice of default, notice of sale, or conduct a trustee's sale while the complete first lien loan modification application is pending, and until the borrower has been provided with a written determination by the mortgage servicer regarding that borrower's eligibility for the requested loan modification." Section 2923.6 also sets out a longer sequence of follow-on protections not quoted here — including a borrower's right to appeal a denial and specific content requirements for a denial notice — that apply only where Section 2923.6 itself applies (see the scope/exemption clause of this sheet); Section 2924.18(a)'s dual-tracking prohibition applies more broadly and is not subject to that same carve-out.

expectedJSON.body: California Civil Code § 2923.7(a) requires: "When a borrower requests a foreclosure prevention alternative, the mortgage servicer shall promptly establish a single point of contact and provide to the borrower one or more direct means of communication with the single point of contact." The single point of contact is a defined role with specific statutory duties, not merely a named individual: it must, among other things, communicate the application process and deadlines, coordinate receipt of application documents, stay informed of the current status of the borrower's foreclosure prevention alternative, ensure the borrower is considered for all alternatives the servicer offers, and — as Section 2923.7(b)(5) specifically provides — have "access to individuals with the ability and authority to stop foreclosure proceedings when necessary." The single point of contact must remain assigned to the borrower's account until the servicer determines that all loss mitigation options have been exhausted or the account becomes current, and the servicer must ensure the single point of contact refers the borrower to a supervisor on request, if the single point of contact has one. Whether Example Loan Servicing, Inc. has established a single point of contact for Pat Morgan in connection with the loan secured by 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 is not addressed by this sheet.

expectedJSON.body: Not every mortgage servicer is subject to every Homeowner Bill of Rights provision described in this sheet. Civil Code § 2924.18(b) defines two categories of smaller-volume servicers to which certain sections apply on different terms. The first category, under paragraph (1), is: "A depository institution chartered under state or federal law, a person licensed pursuant to Division 9 (commencing with Section 22000) or Division 20 (commencing with Section 50000) of the Financial Code, or a person licensed pursuant to Part 1 (commencing with Section 10000) of Division 4 of the Business and Professions Code, that, during its immediately preceding annual reporting period, as established with its primary regulator, foreclosed on 175 or fewer residential real properties, containing no more than four dwelling units, that are located in California." The second category, under paragraph (2), is: "A person or entity that services seven or fewer loans encumbering residential real property located in California in a calendar year." A separately numbered section, Civil Code § 2923.6(i), then carves entities meeting that definition out of the dual-tracking and appeal provisions described elsewhere in this sheet: "Subdivisions (c) to (h), inclusive, shall not apply to entities described in subdivision (b) of Section 2924.18." California Civil Code § 2924.18(c) further provides that if a small servicer within the meaning of paragraph (1) later exceeds the 175-foreclosure threshold, it must notify its primary regulator and any delinquent borrower of the date — the first day of the sixth month after the close of the relevant reporting period — on which it becomes subject to Sections 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, and 2924.12. Whether Example Loan Servicing, Inc. falls within either category described in Section 2924.18(b), and therefore whether the dual-tracking, single-point-of-contact, and related provisions described in this sheet reach the servicing of the loan secured by 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, is not addressed by this sheet.

expectedJSON.body: California Civil Code § 2924.12 creates a private right of action for a material violation of certain Homeowner Bill of Rights provisions, and the remedy available differs depending on whether a trustee's sale has already occurred. Before a sale, Section 2924.12(a)(1) provides: "If a trustee's deed upon sale has not been recorded, a borrower may bring an action for injunctive relief to enjoin a material violation of Section 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, or 2924.17." Any such injunction remains in place until the violation is corrected and remedied. After a trustee's deed upon sale has been recorded, Section 2924.12(b) instead provides a damages remedy: "a mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall be liable to a borrower for actual economic damages pursuant to Section 3281, resulting from a material violation of Section 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, or 2924.17 by that mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent where the violation was not corrected and remedied prior to the recordation of the trustee's deed upon sale. If the court finds that the material violation was intentional or reckless, or resulted from willful misconduct by a mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent, the court may award the borrower the greater of treble actual damages or statutory damages of fifty thousand dollars ($50,000)." A prevailing borrower may also recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs, and a violation of the listed sections by certain state-licensed persons is separately deemed a violation of that person's licensing law.
